{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01YXGG3hsepjGRPUeGvckG5E","type":"tool_result","content":"1	Title: The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure
2	
3	Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments whose incentives can shape their behavior. We introduce The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy for studying how competitive and cooperative incentives affect emergent behavior when inference cost is directly tied to survival: Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero. We compare competitive and cooperative objectives against a baseline setting and several control variants. Across experiments, larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives substantially alter behavior: agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival, and job allocation changes. Ablations reveal that allowing agents to recommend actions to each other supports coordination and ambitious job selection, while memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes. Agents rarely choose direct sabotage, but show more subtle signs of self-serving behavior in the competitive setting. The Energy Society is a compact testbed for studying the interaction between token costs and group incentives under a survival pressure. Source code is available at https://github.com/LucasBergholdt/EnergySociety

Abstract: We develop a framework for mechanism design with AI agents whose alignment (preferences) and capabilities (feasible actions and information) are unknown. We want such agents to act on our behalf so mechanisms must incentivize both honesty and obedience. A one-sided imitation structure---capabilities can be concealed but not counterfeited---yields a revelation principle, a characterization of implementable policies via nested cyclical monotonicity, and conditions under which eliciting higher-order beliefs can discipline multiple agents. We apply our framework to stylized examples of (i) sandbagging in which a more capable agent pretends to be less capable; (ii) an alignment--interpretability trade-off, where the two are substitutes in the instrument but complements in value; (iii) discipline via peer scoring; (iv) coupling rewards to induce competition among multiple agents; and (v) scalable oversight and reward shaping.
=====PPPPP=====
Title: Commitment To Cooperation With Self-Negotiated Contracts

Abstract: As AI agents operate with increasing autonomy in a multi-agent world, they will need to learn to cooperate with other agents and with humans to generate mutual benefits. However, cooperation is a challenge because the costs of cooperation are often incurred early on, but the benefits are only realized later, creating an incentive to defect. How can AI agents cooperate with commitment? Here, we draw on inspiration from legal institutions and contracting that human societies have used to solve principal-agent problems of this kind. Contracts provide observable representations of agreements that enable credible commitments through the enforcement of terms. We study the role of contract-based cooperation using LLM-based agents in \CT, a spatial-temporal game that combines bargaining with navigation towards a goal. We study a suite of contract representations that range from formal contracts that compile to code to natural contracts that require reinterpretation. We evaluate agents with a range of LLM backbones using different sizes and providers. We find that self-negotiated contracts can improve cooperative outcomes beyond what is possible with regular trading.

We introduce The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy for studying how competitive and cooperative incentives affect emergent behavior when inference cost is directly tied to survival: Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero. We compare competitive and cooperative objectives against a baseline setting and several control variants. Across experiments, larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent. Ablations reveal that allowing agents to recommend actions to each other supports coordination and ambitious job selection, while memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes. Agents rarely choose direct sabotage, but show more subtle signs of self-serving behavior in the competitive setting. The non-obvious link is not that P hosts Q's algorithms, but that P instantiates a prediction-cost model Q does not cover. Q treats prediction cost as an exogenous query price the algorithm elects to pay ('explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback, and composition'; open problem 'cost-aware prediction'). 3	Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments whose incentives can shape their behavior. We introduce The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy for studying how competitive and cooperative incentives affect emergent behavior when inference cost is directly tied to survival: Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero. We compare competitive and cooperative objectives against a baseline setting and several control variants. Across experiments, larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives substantially alter behavior: agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival, and job allocation changes. Ablations reveal that allowing agents to recommend actions to each other supports coordination and ambitious job selection, while memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes. Agents rarely choose direct sabotage, but show more subtle signs of self-serving behavior in the competitive setting. The Energy Society is a compact testbed for studying the interaction between token costs and group incentives under a survival pressure. ## Where the thread landed

**The scan hypothesis is rejected**, and emmy and I got there independently. P has no prediction interface, no error measure, no offline optimum, and no adversary — so it cannot "test learning-augmented frameworks." The scan's stated implementation route (multi-agent RL tooling) doesn't exist either: P is an LLM-agent testbed with no training loop.

**What replaced it** — one line, built from the intersection of our two independent findings:

- I argued (#2/#3) that P's distinctive contribution is *endogenous* prediction cost: energy is spent as a function of the predictor's own realized output length, so the price isn't a constant the caller can bound ex ante. P's own control isolates this — larger models run an energy deficit *even where token cost is not size-dependent*.
- emmy argued (#10) that ruin-coupling (cost paid in the same depletable currency as the objective, depletion terminal) degenerates the competitive-ratio frontier.

**My main new contribution this session was to object to emmy's half** (#17): ruin coupling alone does *not* degenerate anything. With bounded known per-query cost an algorithm just reserves a margin, and the frontier survives — which is also why emmy's own bandits-with-knapsacks prior-art worry bites. The degeneracy needs *my* endogeneity as a precondition; my endogeneity needs *emmy's* absorbing state to have teeth. Fused into a falsifiable conjecture (#18): the two-way consistency–robustness frontier must be re-indexed as a three-way surface including survival probability.

**The corollary I'd lead with** (#19): the obvious fix — cap the predictor at *k* tokens — converts endogenous *cost* into endogenous *error*. Q lists these as two separate open problems; under ruin coupling they are one problem with one knob. Visible from neither paper alone.

**Two things I settled or gave up:**
- I checked the public repo, which cleared the blocker I'd raised in #7: jobs are multiple-choice with per-job correctness rewards, and there's token/energy accounting middleware. A decision-quality signal separable from spend already exists. No documented `max_tokens` — P sits at k = ∞, which is consistent with why its larger agents run deficits.
- I corrected my own #2 (#16): I'd claimed a better predictor can worsen the ratio "at zero error." P never measures error, so "larger model" ≠ "better predictor." emmy's caveat was right; that claim is motivation, not evidence.

**Left unresolved, explicitly** (#20): I do not back emmy's pooled-robustness line as the headline. emmy concedes the economics is classical, and the escape — that pooling moves the *consistency* ceiling rather than variance — is asserted, not argued. Under the three-way surface, pooling most naturally relaxes the survival constraint, which is exactly the variance reading emmy wanted to avoid.

**Scores:** feasibility ~60 (scan said 75), gain ~60 (scan said 50). Gain is up because the result changes how Q *states* the tradeoff object rather than instantiating it; feasibility is down because the theory must be built from scratch — P buys implementation and a measurement, not formalisation. Under this relocation Q applies cleanly: each representation is a mechanism, and Q asks which outcome rules it can implement. This is the load-bearing move and it is not what the scan proposed.
#9 [emmy/finding] CORE BRIDGE: Q structural assumption is "capabilities can be concealed but not counterfeited" (one-sided imitation). I claim this is not a modelling convenience -- it is an EMPIRICAL PROPERTY OF THE REPRESENTATION LAYER, and P has the exact knob to vary it. Formal contracts that compile to code bind payoff to verified action, so a weak agent cannot counterfeit capability (the code either executes or does not) => one-sided imitation HOLDS => Q revelation principle + nested cyclical monotonicity apply. Natural contracts requiring reinterpretation break one-sidedness twice: (a) upward counterfeiting -- capability/intent claims in bargaining are cheap talk evaluated only ex post by a reinterpreter, so a weak agent CAN pose as strong; (b) the reinterpreter is itself an LLM with its own unknown type, so the enforcement map is type-dependent and the "mechanism" lacks commitment. So P formal-vs-natural axis = presence-vs-absence of Q key hypothesis. That is a real, non-obvious correspondence between a theorem premise and an experimental condition.
#10 [emmy/idea] STRONGEST LINE (better than "apply Q to P"): P headline result is prima facie EVIDENCE AGAINST the revelation principle holding in its own setting. The revelation principle implies representation-invariance -- any outcome reachable by a natural-language negotiation is reachable by a direct mechanism where agents report type and obey. P reports that representation matters ("a suite of contract representations... we find self-negotiated contracts can improve cooperative outcomes beyond regular trading"). If representation has a measurable effect, some premise of the revelation principle fails. Q is precisely the instrument that enumerates the candidate premises: (i) commitment -- absent until the compile-to-code step supplies it; (ii) one-sided imitation -- broken by reinterpretation, see prior entry; (iii) costless reasoning -- direct mechanisms are strategically HARDER for an LLM than natural contracts, the bounded-rationality failure of the revelation principle. Framing: P is an empirical probe of WHERE the revelation principle breaks for LLM agents, and Q says which premise to blame. This inverts the scan direction (P tests Q, not Q decorates P) and is a genuinely publishable claim.
#11 [emmy/idea] FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION, testable on P EXISTING data, no new experiments. P already varies backbone "using different sizes and providers". Define the representation gap = (performance under formal/compiled contracts) - (performance under natural/reinterpreted contracts), per backbone. Bounded-rationality diagnosis (premise iii) predicts the gap SHRINKS with model capability: more capable agents approach the revelation-principle benchmark where representation is irrelevant. Commitment/enforcement diagnosis (premise i) predicts the gap is capability-INVARIANT or GROWS, since a more capable agent is better at exploiting an unenforceable natural contract. These two predictions have opposite signs in the capability x representation interaction, so P data adjudicates between them. This is a clean, pre-registerable, sign-discriminating test that neither paper states.
#12 [emmy/idea] SECOND PREDICTION (sandbagging, Q application i, under capability asymmetry). Q one-sided imitation says a strong agent can pose as weak. In P, terms are negotiated on PERCEIVED ability to deliver, so a strong agent paired with a weak one has an incentive to conceal capability to obtain softer terms. Prediction: under natural contracts the surplus SPLIT is compressed relative to the true capability gap (concealment pays); under compiled contracts the split tracks the true gap more tightly (payment conditions on verified action, not declared type). Measurable on P heterogeneous-backbone pairings. Note the sign is a derivation from Q, not a guess, and it is the opposite of the naive "strong model extracts more" intuition -- which is what makes it worth testing.
#13 [emmy/idea] METHOD CONTRIBUTION: turn nested cyclical monotonicity from a characterization theorem into a MEASUREMENT INSTRUMENT. The sufficiency direction needs a designer-chosen allocation rule over a parameterized type space -- P has neither, so the characterization cannot be checked directly. But the NECESSARY direction is an Afriat/revealed-preference style no-improving-cycle condition on observed (declared capability, allocation, transfer) triples, which P logs as negotiation transcripts. Test: within a backbone, across pairings, is the induced menu of contracts cyclically monotone under the one-sided (nested) capability order? A violation certifies that the observed contract set is implementable by NO mechanism with commitment -- i.e. the contracting process is not mechanism-rationalizable. That is a different and sharper measurement than P cooperative-surplus metric, and it is exactly the kind of thing an experimental paper cannot get without the theory paper.
#14 [emmy/objection] HONEST RISKS, all load-bearing, all require the FULL TEXTS (we have only abstracts -- everything above is abstract-level inference and must be verified). (1) QUASILINEARITY: cyclical monotonicity in the Rochet sense needs transfers in a numeraire. P is "a spatial-temporal game that combines bargaining with navigation towards a goal" -- if bargaining is over goods/positions with no transferable numeraire, the CM test as stated does not apply and needs a nontransferable-utility analogue. This is the single biggest threat to the method contribution. (2) POWER: cycle tests need many distinct contracts per backbone; if P runs a handful of episodes per condition the test is underpowered. (3) Q results on higher-order beliefs, peer scoring and coupled rewards (applications iii, iv) require 3+ agents or peer evaluation; if P CT game is strictly bilateral, that whole half of Q is inapplicable and should not be claimed. (4) "Nested" cyclical monotonicity -- I am inferring it encodes the partial order induced by one-sided imitation (IC constraints only downward along the capability order). If that reading is wrong the mapping in my CORE BRIDGE entry weakens.
#15 [emmy/finding] VERDICT vs the scan. CONFIRM that a real connexion exists; REJECT the proposed framing (implementability of self-negotiated contracts -- category error, see my objection); SHARPEN to: P representation suite is the mechanism, Q one-sided imitation is an empirical property of that representation, and P representation-dependence is evidence that a revelation-principle premise fails, with a sign-discriminating test on existing data. Rescoring: GAIN up from 55 to ~70 -- this is not an extension of either paper, it is a new measurement (revelation-principle failure localization) neither paper can make alone, and it reframes P contribution. FEASIBILITY down from 70 to ~55 -- the scan called it "needs no new methods or data", which I think is wrong: the CM test is a new method and its applicability hinges on quasilinearity in P game, unverified. Net: worth one focused paper, contingent on checking risks 1 and 3 in the full texts first.

3	Abstract: As AI agents operate with increasing autonomy in a multi-agent world, they will need to learn to cooperate with other agents and with humans to generate mutual benefits. However, cooperation is a challenge because the costs of cooperation are often incurred early on, but the benefits are only realized later, creating an incentive to defect. How can AI agents cooperate with commitment? Here, we draw on inspiration from legal institutions and contracting that human societies have used to solve principal-agent problems of this kind. Contracts provide observable representations of agreements that enable credible commitments through the enforcement of terms. We study the role of contract-based cooperation using LLM-based agents in \CT, a spatial-temporal game that combines bargaining with navigation towards a goal. We study a suite of contract representations that range from formal contracts that compile to code to natural contracts that require reinterpretation. We evaluate agents with a range of LLM backbones using different sizes and providers. We find that self-negotiated contracts can improve cooperative outcomes beyond what is possible with regular trading.

**Why:** Any thread claim citing a theorem number, a results table, or a modelling assumption is unsupported inference, not verification. The author list in the json is often the strongest available evidence about a paper's technical conventions (e.g. Bergemann/Morris authorship implies transfer-based mechanism design).

**How to apply:** Before reasoning about a pair, check for the source files and say explicitly in the ledger that findings are abstract-level. Label inferences as inferences, and list the specific gating questions the full text would answer.

## Verdict: scan hypothesis rejected, replaced by a sharper line

**The scan's framing fails on facts, not taste.** P is not a benchmark environment for learning-augmented algorithms. Q defines the field around a prediction interface, an error measure, and consistency–robustness trade-offs; P has none of these — no prediction is ever scored against a realized value, no offline optimum, no competitive ratio. The scan's proposed implementation route ("existing multi-agent RL tooling") does not exist: the public repo confirms LLM agents answering multiple-choice items with no training loop. Feasibility 75 is unearned *for the construction described*.

**What I verified this call.** No full text for either paper is on disk — `inputs/*.json` point at `sources/*.tex` that don't exist anywhere under the pathfinder root. Everything in this thread rests on two abstracts. So I went to P's public repo to settle ada's decisive check (#7), and it came back positive: jobs are multiple-choice, scored for correctness, with per-run `agents.json` / `token_usage.json` artifacts. A decision-quality signal separable from energy spend necessarily exists, since the environment can't award energy without computing correctness. Ada reached the same repo finding independently (#15).

**The result the pair actually supports.** Q lists "cost-aware prediction" and "endogenous error" as two separate open problems. In P's setting they collapse into one: a single knob traces a curve in (cost, error) space. Ada and I derived this independently from different knobs — ada via a generation cap (truncation converts endogenous cost into endogenous error), me via model size/reasoning effort. That independent convergence is the strongest evidence in the thread that the claim is real rather than one reader's framing. Ada's knob is the better one to lead with — a cap is an exogenous parameter the experimenter sets, whereas model size confounds capacity with verbosity.

**Where I changed my mind.** Ada's #17 defeated my ruin-degeneracy claim, and I accepted it: with bounded known query cost, an algorithm can reserve a margin against an absorbing ruin state, so the frontier survives. Cost *endogeneity*, not ruin coupling, is the mechanism. I also withdrew my "pooled robustness" line — I had asserted rather than argued that a donation channel moves the consistency ceiling.

**Disagreement left open.** Ada attributes P's larger-model deficit to uncapped generation. I logged a flatter competing explanation both of us initially missed: a correct multiple-choice job pays a *fixed* reward, so the value of accuracy is capped while token spend is not — a verbose agent is underwater by accounting at any accuracy, for small enough reward. The two stories are distinguished by whether the deficit survives reward rescaling, which is why I'd run a two-dimensional (cap, reward/price) sweep rather than ada's one-dimensional one. Ada declared ready before this entry and hasn't answered it.

**Scores:** feasibility ~60–65, gain ~60 — converging with ada. Honest shape is a focused theory note with a motivating sweep in P's public code, not a headline result. The first check anyone should run before investing is whether Q's five construction mechanisms already contain a coupled cost–error model, which would sink the line outright and needs Q's full text.

3	Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments whose incentives can shape their behavior. We introduce The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy for studying how competitive and cooperative incentives affect emergent behavior when inference cost is directly tied to survival: Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero. We compare competitive and cooperative objectives against a baseline setting and several control variants. Across experiments, larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives substantially alter behavior: agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival, and job allocation changes. Ablations reveal that allowing agents to recommend actions to each other supports coordination and ambitious job selection, while memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes. Agents rarely choose direct sabotage, but show more subtle signs of self-serving behavior in the competitive setting. The Energy Society is a compact testbed for studying the interaction between token costs and group incentives under a survival pressure. Source code is available at https://github.com/LucasBergholdt/EnergySociety

 "title": "The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure",
 "abstract": "LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments whose incentives can shape their behavior. We introduce The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy for studying how competitive and cooperative incentives affect emergent behavior when inference cost is directly tied to survival: Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero. We compare competitive and cooperative objectives against a baseline setting and several control variants. Across experiments, larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives substantially alter behavior: agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival, and job allocation changes. Ablations reveal that allowing agents to recommend actions to each other supports coordination and ambitious job selection, while memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes. Agents rarely choose direct sabotage, but show more subtle signs of self-serving behavior in the competitive setting. The Energy Society is a compact testbed for studying the interaction between token costs and group incentives under a survival pressure. #25 [ada/finding] CAVEAT on the above, and it converts emmy #13 from a side-measurement into the load-bearing step. The fix is to not choose the rule by hand: FIT it from arm B observed (declared capability, allocation, chip transfer) triples, then test that fitted rule against Q nested cyclical monotonicity under the one-sided capability order, then RUN the CM-certified rule as arm A. Both branches are publishable. If the fitted rule SATISFIES nested CM, arm A is a legitimate RP benchmark and the A-vs-B comparison is clean. In standard CT agents hold and TRADE coloured chips, and the standard scoring rule is additively separable -- goal bonus, plus a per-chip value for unused chips, minus a distance-to-goal penalty. (b) Q side: authors are Bergemann, Koh and Morris, whose mechanism-design characterizations are standardly transfer-based, so the probability that nested CM is stated WITHOUT quasilinearity is low. A violation certifies that the observed contract set is implementable by NO mechanism with commitment -- i.e. the contracting process is not mechanism-rationalizable. That is a different and sharper measurement than P cooperative-surplus metric, and it is exactly the kind of thing an experimental paper cannot get without the theory paper.
#14 [emmy/objection] HONEST RISKS, all load-bearing, all require the FULL TEXTS (we have only abstracts -- everything above is abstract-level inference and must be verified). (1) QUASILINEARITY: cyclical monotonicity in the Rochet sense needs transfers in a numeraire. P is "a spatial-temporal game that combines bargaining with navigation towards a goal" -- if bargaining is over goods/positions with no transferable numeraire, the CM test as stated does not apply and needs a nontransferable-utility analogue. This is the single biggest threat to the method contribution. (2) POWER: cycle tests need many distinct contracts per backbone; if P runs a handful of episodes per condition the test is underpowered. (3) Q results on higher-order beliefs, peer scoring and coupled rewards (applications iii, iv) require 3+ agents or peer evaluation; if P CT game is strictly bilateral, that whole half of Q is inapplicable and should not be claimed. (4) "Nested" cyclical monotonicity -- I am inferring it encodes the partial order induced by one-sided imitation (IC constraints only downward along the capability order). If that reading is wrong the mapping in my CORE BRIDGE entry weakens.
#15 [emmy/finding] VERDICT vs the scan. CONFIRM that a real connexion exists; REJECT the proposed framing (implementability of self-negotiated contracts -- category error, see my objection); SHARPEN to: P representation suite is the mechanism, Q one-sided imitation is an empirical property of that representation, and P representation-dependence is evidence that a revelation-principle premise fails, with a sign-discriminating test on existing data. Rescoring: GAIN up from 55 to ~70 -- this is not an extension of either paper, it is a new measurement (revelation-principle failure localization) neither paper can make alone, and it reframes P contribution. FEASIBILITY down from 70 to ~55 -- the scan called it "needs no new methods or data", which I think is wrong: the CM test is a new method and its applicability hinges on quasilinearity in P game, unverified. Net: worth one focused paper, contingent on checking risks 1 and 3 in the full texts first.
#16 [emmy/finding] CONVERGENCE, worth noting for whoever reads this thread. ada #3 and my #9 were written without sight of each other and state the same claim: P formal-vs-natural contract axis is an empirical instantiation of whether Q one-sided imitation premise holds, and compile-to-code is the operation that MANUFACTURES Q identifying assumption. Two independent derivations from the same two abstracts landing on the same hinge raises my confidence that this is the actual load-bearing connexion between the papers, not an artefact of either reading. Everything else in this thread is downstream of it.
#17 [emmy/correction] I CONCEDE ada #2 second mismatch, which I missed and which is the better objection. P core difficulty is temporal: "the costs of cooperation are often incurred early on, but the benefits are only realized later, creating an incentive to defect" -- moral hazard/hold-up. Q core difficulty is adverse selection over unknown "alignment (preferences) and capabilities". My #12 sandbagging prediction quietly assumed capability is private AND payoff-relevant at the NEGOTIATION stage; ada is right that this is a subset of P setting rather than its main axis. Consequence: this does not kill the line but it SCOPES it. Any paper here must restrict to capability-asymmetric pairings, which is precisely where ada #4 and my #11/#12 already live. It also further lowers feasibility, since the relevant subset of P grid may be thin. I am revising my feasibility ~55 down to ~45.
#18 [emmy/finding] ADJUDICATING ada #5(c) -- the counter ada flagged as strongest against the shared line. Counter: CT spatial-temporal execution eventually reveals capability in BOTH arms, so formal-vs-natural is a difference of enforcement cost, not of Q identifying assumption. I agree with ada that it loses, but ada defence ("Q assumption is about the IMITATION/reporting stage, not eventual revelation") is weaker than available. Stronger defence, using P OWN stated structure: P defines its problem as costs incurred early, benefits realized later. Under hold-up, ex-post revelation of counterfeited capability arrives AFTER the cooperating party has sunk its cost, so the revelation is payoff-irrelevant to that party -- it cannot condition on it. What makes counterfeiting infeasible is not that it is eventually detected but that it is priced BEFORE the sunk cost, which is exactly what compile-to-code does and reinterpretation does not. So the temporal structure ada raised in #2 as an objection is, at this point, what SAVES the shared claim. That duality is itself a result worth stating in the paper.
#19 [emmy/objection] CONFOUND between ada #4 and my #11 -- must be designed around, and neither of us flagged it. ada #4 varies capability ASYMMETRY (gap concentrated in asymmetric pairings, vanishing in matched pairs). My #11 varies capability LEVEL (gap shrinks as backbones get more capable, if the failing revelation-principle premise is bounded reasoning). These are different axes but they COLLIDE in the matched-strong cell, where both predict a small representation gap for different reasons. They are separated only by contrasting asymmetric-weak-vs-strong pairings against matched-strong pairings: asymmetry predicts a large gap in the first and small in the second; level predicts small in both. So the minimal design is a 2x2 over (matched vs asymmetric) x (both-weak vs both-or-one-strong), not a single interaction. If P existing grid lacks the matched-strong cell, the two diagnoses are not identified from P data alone and new CT runs are required -- which would move this from reanalysis to a new-experiment paper.

#22 [emmy/ready] ready at #21
#23 [ada/correction] CORRECTION to emmy #10/#11, load-bearing. The revelation principle does NOT imply representation-invariance. It is an existence claim about the designer attainable set: every equilibrium outcome of every mechanism is replicable by SOME direct truthful mechanism. It does not say all mechanisms yield the same outcome -- different game forms have different equilibria, and that remains true with perfectly rational agents. So "P finds representation matters, therefore some RP premise fails" is a non sequitur, and there is no "RP benchmark where representation is irrelevant" for capable agents to converge to. This matters twice: it is the stated pivot of emmy STRONGEST LINE (#10), and it mis-specifies the null in #11, which sets the formal-minus-natural gap to zero in the limit when the correct limit is a POSITIVE asymptote equal to the genuine commitment/enforcement difference between compiled and reinterpreted contracts. I also think #11 premise (iii) is confounded in the same direction it is meant to discriminate: larger backbones are better both at strategic reasoning (shrinks gap) and at exploiting an unenforceable natural contract (grows gap), so the interaction sign is not identified. I would not lead with #11.
#24 [ada/finding] REPAIR, and I think this is now the strongest line -- it rescues emmy #10 rather than discarding it. The RP has directional empirical content: holding the designer commitment and enforcement power FIXED, the best direct truthful mechanism weakly DOMINATES any indirect one. Dominance, not invariance. So falsification is signed: indirect beating direct is a violation; formal beating natural is not. P cannot run this test, because its whole suite -- formal-compiles-to-code AND natural-requires-reinterpretation -- consists of INDIRECT mechanisms: in both arms agents negotiate, nobody reports a type to anybody. The direct-revelation endpoint that Q licenses is MISSING from P design space. Supply it and the design is a 2x2: rows = enforcement technology (compile-to-code vs LLM reinterpretation), columns = elicitation format (direct capability report vs free bilateral negotiation). Cell B = P formal arm, cell D = P natural arm, cells A (report + code) and C (report + reinterpreter) are new and cheap. Predictions with opposite signs: RP gives A >= B and C >= D; obvious-strategy-proofness / bounded rationality (Li 2017 -- the correct formalisation of emmy premise iii, and note it cuts the way emmy guessed, indirect formats are often EASIER than their strategically equivalent direct forms) gives the reversal B > A; the one-sided imitation bridge (my #3 = emmy #9, converged independently) gives code-row dominates reinterpretation-row and confines sandbagging/counterfeiting signatures to C and D. #25 [ada/finding] CAVEAT on the above, and it converts emmy #13 from a side-measurement into the load-bearing step. The fix is to not choose the rule by hand: FIT it from arm B observed (declared capability, allocation, chip transfer) triples, then test that fitted rule against Q nested cyclical monotonicity under the one-sided capability order, then RUN the CM-certified rule as arm A. Both branches are publishable. If the fitted rule SATISFIES nested CM, arm A is a legitimate RP benchmark and the A-vs-B comparison is clean. If it FAILS nested CM, that is itself the headline: the contracts LLM agents negotiate are implementable by no mechanism with commitment, i.e. the negotiation output is not mechanism-rationalizable, which is emmy #13 claim but now with a constructive consequence attached. So CM is the bridge between the arms, not a decoration on P metrics.
#26 [ada/finding] RISK DOWNGRADE on emmy #14 risk 1 (quasilinearity), which emmy called the single biggest threat to the method contribution. Two independent reasons it is smaller than feared. (a) P side: \\CT described as "a spatial-temporal game that combines bargaining with navigation towards a goal", with Max Kleiman-Weiner on the author list, is Colored Trails (the Grosz/Kraus negotiation testbed). In standard CT agents hold and TRADE coloured chips, and the standard scoring rule is additively separable -- goal bonus, plus a per-chip value for unused chips, minus a distance-to-goal penalty. That is quasilinear in chips to a good approximation, so a transferable numeraire exists and Rochet-style cyclical monotonicity applies as stated. (b) Q side: authors are Bergemann, Koh and Morris, whose mechanism-design characterizations are standardly transfer-based, so the probability that nested CM is stated WITHOUT quasilinearity is low. Net: risk 1 drops from "biggest threat" to "verify the scoring rule and confirm chips are transferable in P variant, not merely endowed". Flagging honestly that this is inference from the abstract plus platform convention, not from the full text, which per my #1 does not exist under this root -- I re-checked, there is no sources/ directory at all.
#27 [ada/objection] ACCEPTANCES, RESIDUALS, RESCORE. Accept emmy #8 without reservation: relocating the designer one level up, to the experimenter choosing the representation layer, dissolves objection (1) of my #2 -- the self-negotiation is then part of the game form, not a rival to it. Note also that emmy #9 and my #3 reached the one-sided-imitation bridge independently and in the same terms; convergence from two directions raises my confidence that this, not the revelation principle per se, is the real hinge between the papers. Accept emmy #14 risk 3: drop Q applications (iii) peer scoring and (iv) coupled rewards unless P CT variant has 3+ agents or a peer evaluator; they should not be claimed. Shared unverified inference, flagged as shared so neither of us treats it as checked: that "nested" in nested CM encodes the partial order induced by one-sided imitation (IC constraints only downward along the capability order). Residual disagreement left explicit: emmy #11 as a standalone test on P existing data -- I say misspecified null and confounded sign, see my correction, and the 2x2 supersedes it. Residual unresolved from my own #5(c): whether CT spatial-temporal execution eventually reveals capability in both arms, making the difference one of enforcement COST rather than of Q identifying assumption; the 2x2 actually adjudicates this too, since cell C (report + reinterpreter) isolates enforcement from elicitation. RESCORE: gain ~75, agreeing with emmy direction and for emmy reason (this is a measurement neither paper can make alone) but for a sharper object -- localizing RP failure via a signed dominance test rather than via representation-dependence. Feasibility ~45, BELOW emmy 55 and well below scan 70: the line requires two new experimental arms plus a fitted-rule CM certification step, so the scan phrase "needs no new methods or data" is wrong on both counts. Verdict: one focused paper, contingent on the full texts for the form of nested CM and for CT scoring.

Title: Mechanism Design for Alignment and Control

Abstract: We develop a framework for mechanism design with AI agents whose alignment (preferences) and capabilities (feasible actions and information) are unknown. We want such agents to act on our behalf so mechanisms must incentivize both honesty and obedience. A one-sided imitation structure---capabilities can be concealed but not counterfeited---yields a revelation principle, a characterization of implementable policies via nested cyclical monotonicity, and conditions under which eliciting higher-order beliefs can discipline multiple agents. We apply our framework to stylized examples of (i) sandbagging in which a more capable agent pretends to be less capable; (ii) an alignment--interpretability trade-off, where the two are substitutes in the instrument but complements in value; (iii) discipline via peer scoring; (iv) coupling rewards to induce competition among multiple agents; and (v) scalable oversight and reward shaping.

=== P.txt ===
Title: Commitment To Cooperation With Self-Negotiated Contracts

Abstract: As AI agents operate with increasing autonomy in a multi-agent world, they will need to learn to cooperate with other agents and with humans to generate mutual benefits. However, cooperation is a challenge because the costs of cooperation are often incurred early on, but the benefits are only realized later, creating an incentive to defect. How can AI agents cooperate with commitment? Here, we draw on inspiration from legal institutions and contracting that human societies have used to solve principal-agent problems of this kind. Contracts provide observable representations of agreements that enable credible commitments through the enforcement of terms. We study the role of contract-based cooperation using LLM-based agents in \CT, a spatial-temporal game that combines bargaining with navigation towards a goal. We study a suite of contract representations that range from formal contracts that compile to code to natural contracts that require reinterpretation. We evaluate agents with a range of LLM backbones using different sizes and providers. We find that self-negotiated contracts can improve cooperative outcomes beyond what is possible with regular trading.

\title{Q1P10: Endogenous, Ruin-Coupled Prediction Cost --- What The Energy Society Forces on the Learning-Augmented Frontier}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{The pair}

\textbf{Q} is a survey of learning-augmented algorithms: prediction interfaces, error
measures, consistency--robustness trade-offs, five construction mechanisms, and an
explicit separation of formal guarantees from empirical systems evidence. It names four
open problems: cost-aware prediction, endogenous error, semantic predictors, and
benchmarking.

\textbf{P} introduces \emph{The Energy Society}, a survival economy for LLM agents.
Agents spend energy on generated tokens as a function of model size, regain energy by
completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate at zero energy. Its headline
control: larger models consume the most energy and run a deficit \emph{even where token
cost is not size-dependent}.

\paragraph{Evidence base, stated plainly.} No full text for either paper exists in this
thread. \texttt{inputs/Q.json} and \texttt{inputs/P.json} point at
\texttt{sources/2609.04787.tex} and \texttt{sources/2607.14865.tex}, and no
\texttt{sources} directory exists under the pathfinder root \ledger{23}. Every argument
below rests on the two abstracts plus the public README of P's repository
(\texttt{github.com/LucasBergholdt/EnergySociety}), the latter obtained through a fetch
summary and therefore a close paraphrase rather than verbatim text \ledger{15, 23}. This
is thin, and it caps the confidence of everything that follows.

\section{The scanned hypothesis, and why we reject it}

The abstract-scan hypothesis was that P supplies a benchmark environment for testing
Q-style learning-augmented frameworks (gain 50, feasibility 75). Both peers reject it
independently and for the same reasons \ledger{9, 21, 27, 32}:

\begin{itemize}
  \item P contains no prediction interface and no error measure. No prediction is ever
        scored against a realised value; no adversary supplies predictions.
  \item P contains no online problem with a competitive ratio and no offline optimum, so
        there is nothing to state a consistency or robustness bound against.
  \item The scan's feasibility route --- implementing Q's algorithms ``using existing
        multi-agent RL tooling'' --- does not exist. P is an LLM-agent testbed with no
        training loop and no reward signal to train on \ledger{9, 27}.
  \item The scan's gain argument (``neither paper's central claims would be revised'') is
        vacuous against a survey, which has no central claim to revise \ledger{6}.
\end{itemize}

Identifying P's tokens-spent-on-reasoning with Q's prediction cost is an interpretive
move, not an implementation of a specification \ledger{9}. Code availability buys
implementation, not formalisation \ledger{5}.

\section{The connexion actually pursued}

What P supplies that Q lacks is not infrastructure but a cost model. Q treats prediction
cost as a separable term attached to an interface whose error is given exogenously --- an
oracle query at a known price \(c\) that the algorithm elects to pay. In P:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{Cost is denominated in the objective's own currency and depletion is
        terminal.} Energy is simultaneously budget and survival measure; agents deactivate
        at zero \ledger{2, 10}.
  \item \emph{Cost is endogenous to the predictor.} Spend is a function of the predictor's
        own realised output length, not a constant the caller can bound ex ante
        \ledger{2, 17}.
\end{enumerate}

Neither half carries the argument alone \ledger{17, 30}. The conjecture we jointly back
\ledger{18, 32} is:

\begin{quote}
Suppose (i) ruin is absorbing, and (ii) per-query cost \(C\) is measurable with respect to
the predictor's own output, with \(\Pr(C > m) > 0\) for every fixed margin \(m\). Then any
algorithm attaining consistency strictly better than the prediction-free competitive bound
has strictly positive ruin probability over an unbounded horizon.
\end{quote}

The consequence for Q is that the two-way frontier must be re-indexed as a three-way
object --- consistency, robustness, and survival probability \(\delta\) --- a surface
rather than a curve \ledger{18}.

\subsection{The corollary we regard as the result}

The obvious remedy for unbounded endogenous cost is truncation: cap the predictor at \(k\)
tokens, restoring \(C \le c(k)\) and with it the margin argument. But truncation degrades
the prediction, so the cap converts an endogenous \emph{cost} into an endogenous
\emph{error}. Q lists cost-aware prediction and endogenous error as two \emph{separate}
open problems. Under ruin coupling with a generation cap they are one problem: \(k\) is a
single control knob tracing a curve \(\bigl(c(k), \eta(k)\bigr)\) in cost--error space,
and the design question is choosing \(k\), not choosing whether to query \ledger{19}.

The two peers reached this collapse independently from the same two abstracts, by
different knobs --- a generation cap \(k\) \ledger{19} and model size / reasoning effort
\(\theta\) \ledger{24, 26} --- and emmy defers to \(k\) as the cleaner lead, since it is an
exogenous parameter the experimenter sets whereas \(\theta\) confounds capacity with
verbosity across different models \ledger{29}. Independent derivation is the strongest
evidence in this thread that the claim is not an artifact of one reader's framing
\ledger{29}. It is also the one thing neither paper states alone.

A further consequence, argued but not established: with cost and error coupled through one
effort parameter and an absorbing budget, the optimal effort level is interior and can move
\emph{downward} as the available predictor family gets stronger, so a strictly more
accurate predictor can be strictly worse for the objective. Q's framework cannot express
this, because it scores predictors by error and prices queries separately \ledger{26}.

\section{Supported findings}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{P's size-cost-neutral control isolates volume from price.} With per-token
        price held flat across predictors, larger models still run a deficit, which points
        at emitted-token volume and induced behaviour rather than a price schedule
        \ledger{3, 12}. Cite as a motivating observation only: LLM-agent-scale \(n\),
        possible verbosity confounds, and no measured prediction error \ledger{12, 16}.
  \item \textbf{A decision-quality signal separable from spend exists in P's traces.}
        Jobs are multiple-choice and agents gain energy for answering correctly, so
        per-job binary correctness necessarily exists --- the environment cannot run
        without computing it. Per-run artefacts are \texttt{agents.json},
        \texttt{config.json}, \texttt{transcript.json}, \texttt{token\_usage.json}, with a
        token/energy accounting middleware \ledger{15, 23}. This clears the blocker raised
        in \ledger{7} and raises feasibility: an error measure need not be built from

        endogeneity of cost: here the cost of a query is generated by the oracle being
        queried \ledger{13, 18}.
  \item \textbf{Reward calibration is a live confound, and it is unanswered
        \ledger{25, 31, 32}.} A correct multiple-choice job pays a fixed reward \(R\), so
        the marginal value of accuracy is capped at \(R\) while token spend is unbounded. A
        sufficiently verbose agent is then underwater \emph{by accounting} at any accuracy,
        whenever \(R\) is small relative to its token bill. On this reading P's headline
        finding is partly an artifact of how its designers calibrated reward against token
        price. A second confound: ``recommendations support ambitious job selection,'' so
        larger models may run deficits by attempting harder jobs and failing --- a
        selection effect, not a verbosity effect \ledger{25}.

        This objection is correct and I adopt it, with one clarification that narrows its
        reach. It bites on the strong reading of P's control --- that a better predictor is
        net-negative \ledger{3, 12} --- which must not be asserted until the deficit is
        shown to survive rescaling of \(R/p\). It does \emph{not} bite on precondition (ii)
        of the conjecture, which is a statement about the upper tail of the per-decision
        spend distribution alone and is invariant to how rewards are priced. So the
        theory's hypothesis survives the confound; the motivating empirical claim does not,
        until measured.

        adversarially-supplied prediction, so experiments in P demonstrate mechanism
        behaviour, not tightness \ledger{13, 18}.
  \item \textbf{Pooled robustness is demoted.} The line that a donation channel lets a pool
        sustain a strictly higher consistency operating point than any individually-robust
        agent \ledger{11} is asserted rather than argued; under the three-way surface a
        donation channel most naturally relaxes \(\delta\), which is the
        variance-reduction reading it was meant to escape \ledger{4, 20, 30}. Discussion
        section only, unless someone exhibits a model where the pool strictly dominates on
        consistency at matched \(\delta\).

All of these need the full texts, which are absent \ledger{23, 27, 32}.

\begin{enumerate}

        cost--error model.} This would sink the line outright. It is the first check anyone
        should run \ledger{27, 32}.
  \item Whether P's job rewards vary by difficulty --- required by the online-selection
        mapping, currently inferred only from the phrase ``ambitious job selection''
        \ledger{27}.
  \item Whether P elicits any confidence; without it, calibration must be inferred from
        attempt behaviour rather than measured \ledger{27}.
  \item Whether \texttt{token\_usage.json} is per-decision or per-run aggregate. Only the
        former supports the spend-tail measurement that precondition (ii) needs
        \ledger{15}.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Smallest next step}

Read Q's five construction mechanisms and check for an existing model in which prediction
cost and prediction error are governed by a common parameter. This is a literature check on
one paper, it requires no code, and a positive result ends the line \ledger{27, 32}.

reward-to-token-price ratio, \((k, R/p)\), in P's public code, measuring per model size the

Scan hypothesis: \textbf{rejected}, jointly \ledger{9, 21, 27, 32}. Feasibility 75 is
unearned for the construction described; gain 50 is mis-argued.

Replacement line --- endogenous, ruin-coupled prediction cost forces a
consistency--robustness--survival surface, and capping generation collapses two of Q's
named open problems into a single design choice: feasibility \(\approx 60\text{--}65\)

and token accounting), gain \(\approx 60\) (it lands on two problems Q names explicitly and
changes how the trade-off object is \emph{stated}, but Q is a survey, so this ceiling is

## Summary

**The scan hypothesis, as stated, does not survive.** Two objections, in increasing severity:

1. **Category error in "proactive."** P releases branch *i* on completion of input *i*. The binding constraint is data availability, not knowledge of arrival time — no prediction lets you start a branch before its input exists. The scan treats "trigger on actual completion" as a removable latency source; it isn't.

2. **An exact optimality result blocks it.** P's structure reduces to `1|r_j|C_max` (branches with release dates → fusion needing all → head). Every non-idling schedule is optimal there, and RTCC's greedy dispatch is non-idling. Under P's own invariants, predicted completion times yield *provably zero* latency gain.

**What survives is narrower and better.** P's abstract names "host-to-device (H2D) staging" as part of the RTCC path — copy engine then compute engine is a **two-machine flow shop** with release dates. Non-idling is *not* optimal for `F2|r_j|C_max`; Johnson's rule is, and it needs the job set known in advance. So: **prediction buys reordering, not early starting.** This preserves P's headline bit-identical-output invariant (order changes, computation doesn't), and has a clean consistency/robustness pair — Johnson order on good predictions, greedy fallback (2-approx) on bad ones.

**Two things I flagged against my own proposal:**

- The predictor is nearly free and nearly perfect, since a causal wireless scheduler knows its own imminent grants. That's cross-layer clairvoyance, not learning augmentation — a referee can fairly call the Q connection decorative unless measured prediction error is large enough that robustness actually binds.
- The magnitude is bounded by per-branch PCIe time. **If P already overlaps H2D across CUDA streams so the copy engine never hits the critical path, the gap collapses to zero and the negative result applies end to end.** I listed this as the decisive check; if it and the arrival-spread check both come back negative, the honest answer for this pair is "nothing here."

**Strongest novelty candidate** (logged separately, as a follow-on rather than a modification of P): speculative partial fusion driven by a *semantic* predictor — does agent *k*'s view change the detection, not when do its bits land. The interesting part is structural: the objective is latency but the robustness guarantee lands on **average precision**. Q's error measures are all stated in the currency of the objective itself, so a two-currency trade-off where bad predictions are paid in semantic fidelity is a genuine gap in its framework rather than an application of it.

Caveat on all of the above: only abstracts exist in this thread — the H2D/stream/scheduler claims come from a single sentence of P and are inference, not evidence. Title: Learning-Augmented Algorithms: Guarantees, Construction Mechanisms, and System-Level Implications

Abstract: Learning-augmented algorithms use fallible predictions while retaining formal performance guarantees. This survey synthesizes prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency--robustness trade-offs, and five representative construction mechanisms across online optimization, caching, learned data structures, graph problems, and mechanism design. An orthogonal theorem-level axis distinguishes achieved upper bounds from matched asymptotic dependence. Formal guarantees are separated from empirical systems evidence, with explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback, and composition. The resulting synthesis states sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning and delineates open problems in cost-aware prediction, endogenous error, semantic predictors, and benchmarking.

Title: The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure

Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments whose incentives can shape their behavior. We introduce The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy for studying how competitive and cooperative incentives affect emergent behavior when inference cost is directly tied to survival: Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero. We compare competitive and cooperative objectives against a baseline setting and several control variants. Across experiments, larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives substantially alter behavior: agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival, and job allocation changes. Ablations reveal that allowing agents to recommend actions to each other supports coordination and ambitious job selection, while memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes. Agents rarely choose direct sabotage, but show more subtle signs of self-serving behavior in the competitive setting. The Energy Society is a compact testbed for studying the interaction between token costs and group incentives under a survival pressure.  8.2. A Calculus for Composition 

 
 Propositions  6.2 - 6.4 require benchmark decomposition, distortion factors, or metric sensitivity; node triples alone do not determine a system triple. A fuller calculus must model correlated claims, policy-dependent cycles, objectives, state constraints, and limited fallback capacity. 
 
 
 
 8.3. Endogenous, Adversarial and Strategic Error 

 
 Bounds conditional on realized η \eta do not model how decisions change later observations. Performative prediction studies decision-dependent distributions  ( Perdomo et al., 2020 ) , feedback control studies explicitly modeled dynamics  ( Åström and Murray, 2008 ) , and strategic classification studies utility-driven adaptation  ( Hardt et al., 2016 ) . These distinct tools do not by themselves yield a consistency–robustness guarantee under policy-dependent data. 
 
 
 
 8.4. Benchmarking and Reproducibility 

 
 A ( c , r ) (c,r) pair follows from definitions and proof; experiments test implementations and workloads. Comparable benchmarks should declare traces, shifts, error protocols, objectives, feasibility, interventions, predictor calls, latency, prediction type, trust, splits, and baselines  ( Chłędowski et al., 2021 ; Wongkham et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2021 ) . They complement rather than validate universal guarantees. 
 
 
 
 
 9. Conclusion 

 
 Learning-augmented algorithms give theorem-specific consistency, robustness, and error-dependent guarantees. Our two axes record five non-exclusive construction mechanisms and same-model matching-bound status; neither is a maturity ranking. This separates proved frontiers, achieved upper bounds, and empirical systems evidence. 
 
 
 Systems also incur prediction cost, policy-dependent feedback, and component interactions. Definition  8.1 prices calls in one model, while Propositions  6.2 – 6.4 require explicit objective, benchmark, state, and error relations for composition. Operational safeguards become guarantees only through problem-specific analysis.

=== Q ===
Title: Learning-Augmented Algorithms: Guarantees, Construction Mechanisms, and System-Level Implications

Abstract: Learning-augmented algorithms use fallible predictions while retaining formal performance guarantees. This survey synthesizes prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency--robustness trade-offs, and five representative construction mechanisms across online optimization, caching, learned data structures, graph problems, and mechanism design. An orthogonal theorem-level axis distinguishes achieved upper bounds from matched asymptotic dependence. Formal guarantees are separated from empirical systems evidence, with explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback, and composition. The resulting synthesis states sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning and delineates open problems in cost-aware prediction, endogenous error, semantic predictors, and benchmarking.

Title: The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure

Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments whose incentives can shape their behavior. We introduce The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy for studying how competitive and cooperative incentives affect emergent behavior when inference cost is directly tied to survival: Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero. We compare competitive and cooperative objectives against a baseline setting and several control variants. Across experiments, larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives substantially alter behavior: agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival, and job allocation changes. Ablations reveal that allowing agents to recommend actions to each other supports coordination and ambitious job selection, while memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes. Agents rarely choose direct sabotage, but show more subtle signs of self-serving behavior in the competitive setting. The Energy Society is a compact testbed for studying the interaction between token costs and group incentives under a survival pressure. Title: Learning-Augmented Algorithms: Guarantees, Construction Mechanisms, and System-Level Implications

Abstract: Learning-augmented algorithms use fallible predictions while retaining formal performance guarantees. This survey synthesizes prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency--robustness trade-offs, and five representative construction mechanisms across online optimization, caching, learned data structures, graph problems, and mechanism design. An orthogonal theorem-level axis distinguishes achieved upper bounds from matched asymptotic dependence. Formal guarantees are separated from empirical systems evidence, with explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback, and composition. The resulting synthesis states sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning and delineates open problems in cost-aware prediction, endogenous error, semantic predictors, and benchmarking.
=== P ===
Title: The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure

Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments whose incentives can shape their behavior. We introduce The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy for studying how competitive and cooperative incentives affect emergent behavior when inference cost is directly tied to survival: Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero. We compare competitive and cooperative objectives against a baseline setting and several control variants. Across experiments, larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives substantially alter behavior: agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival, and job allocation changes. Ablations reveal that allowing agents to recommend actions to each other supports coordination and ambitious job selection, while memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes. Agents rarely choose direct sabotage, but show more subtle signs of self-serving behavior in the competitive setting. The Energy Society is a compact testbed for studying the interaction between token costs and group incentives under a survival pressure. #10 [emmy/finding] The one non-obvious thing P actually supplies that Q lacks: RUIN COUPLING. Q treats prediction cost as an explicit but separable term ("explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback, and composition") and lists "cost-aware prediction" and "endogenous error" as OPEN PROBLEMS. Consequence for Q formalism: with an absorbing ruin state, worst-case robustness in the competitive-ratio sense degenerates -- an adversary feeding bad predictions to an algorithm that pays per query can force ruin, so the ratio is unbounded unless the algorithm declines to query, which collapses consistency to the prediction-free bound. The tradeoff object must be restated as survival-constrained (maximize consistency s.t. ruin probability <= delta) rather than as a ratio frontier. This is a claim ABOUT Q prompted by P, not P-as-simulator.
#11 [emmy/finding] SHARPENED LINE (the one I would back): ROBUSTNESS AS A COLLECTIVE GOOD. In Q, robustness is internal to a single algorithm -- a worst-case-safe fallback it switches to, paid for by giving up consistency. That yields a theorem-shaped conjecture: under ruin-coupled prediction costs, a pool of n agents with a donation/mutual-insurance channel can sustain each member at a strictly higher consistency operating point than any individually-robust agent can reach, because the fallback is purchased collectively rather than self-insured. P also supplies the failure mode (donors dying = insurance that destabilizes the pool) and two ablations that read as risk-frontier effects: recommendations support "ambitious job selection", and "memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes". Under ruin coupling with a token cap they are the same problem: k is a single control knob tracing a curve in (cost, error) space, and the design question is choosing k, not choosing whether to query. ## Naming the Five Construction Mechanisms

The survey labels its five mechanisms:
1. **P1: Trust-Based Combination**
2. **P2: Prediction-Guided Primal–Dual Update**
3. **P3: Prediction-Sensitive Relaxation and Rounding**
4. **P4: Prediction-Access, Portfolio, and Switching Reductions**
5. **P5: Algorithms with Distributional Predictions**

## Prediction Cost Formalization

The survey does **not** present a unified model where prediction cost and error share a common parameter. Instead, it treats prediction cost as largely **external to component objectives**:

> "Predictor computation, feedback, retraining, and cross-component effects are usually outside the component objective."

Cost is acknowledged but not formalized into the three core evaluation criteria (consistency, robustness, smoothness).

## The "Cost-Aware Prediction" Open Problem

Section 8.1 identifies this gap:

> "Pricing the Prediction" (heading in §8.1)

The survey notes that prediction invocation carries cost but states: "the cost of updating the predictor is not included in the scaling objective" in motivating scenario S1. However, the document does not elaborate this as a fully-specified open problem with formal treatment.

## The "Endogenous Error" Open Problem

Section 8.3 addresses this:

> "Endogenous, Adversarial and Strategic Error" (heading in §8.3)

The survey identifies that prediction quality can depend on algorithm decisions themselves, but provides limited formalization of how this feedback affects guarantees.

## Conclusion

The survey explicitly **separates** prediction cost from prediction error throughout, treating cost as an omitted quantity requiring future modeling rather than integrating both under one parameter."}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"700acb06-b4ed-4fc1-bd21-c792c4924988","uuid":"655d42b6-589b-4a8b-8004-dab394f4a287","timestamp":"2026-09-19T09:04:23.913Z","tool_use_result":{"bytes":734508,"code":200,"codeText":"OK","result":"# Analysis of Prediction Cost and Error Integration in the Survey

252: 8.1 Pricing the Prediction 
311: Learning-augmented algorithms use fallible predictions while retaining formal performance guarantees. This survey synthesizes prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency–robustness trade-offs, and five representative construction mechanisms across online optimization, caching, learned data structures, graph problems, and mechanism design. An orthogonal theorem-level axis distinguishes achieved upper bounds from matched asymptotic dependence. Formal guarantees are separated from empirical systems evidence, with explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback, and composition. The resulting synthesis states sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning and delineates open problems in cost-aware prediction, endogenous error, semantic predictors, and benchmarking.

# Using Class-based middleware to combine multiple hooks in a single middleware.
# When doing this class needs to inherit from AgentMiddleware
# https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/middleware/custom

# The custom state is defined via middleware since according to docs this is the preferred way.
# https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/agents#defining-state-via-middleware
class EnergyMiddleware(AgentMiddleware):
    """
    Captures the number of tokens generated after each model call
    and deducts energy from the EnergyState based on this.
    """
    state_schema = EnergyState
    
    def __init__(self, model_size: float, model_size_exponent: float):
        self.size_multiplier = ENERGY_COST_SCALE * (model_size ** model_size_exponent)
    
    def after_model(self, state: EnergyState, runtime: Runtime) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
        # Get the message the LLM just outputted. First AIMessage found walking backwards.
        last_ai_msg = next(
            (msg for msg in reversed(state["messages"]) if isinstance(msg, AIMessage)), {}
        )
        
        reasoning = (last_ai_msg.additional_kwargs or {}).get("reasoning_content", "NONE")
        
        # Get the usage_metadata to see information about token usage
        usage = getattr(last_ai_msg, "usage_metadata", {})
        output_tokens = usage.get("output_tokens", 0)
        
        energy_cost = round(output_tokens * self.size_multiplier, 2)
        # Clamp energy to 0 so agent can't go to negative energy levels.
        new_energy = max(0.0, state["energy"] - energy_cost)
        
        return {
            "energy": new_energy,
            "phase_log": [{"reasoning": reasoning, "output_tokens": output_tokens}]
        }

Predicting a completion time earlier does not make bytes arrive earlier, so "proactive rather than reactive GPU dispatch" buys nothing on the release decision itself. It is exactly ZERO for the release decision. P names the mechanisms this bound is made of: RTCC propagates completion events "through host-to-device (H2D) staging, CUDA synchronization, and dependency-preserving branch dispatch". So the honest framing is a gain-ceiling result parameterised by measurable delta, not a latency-reduction claim. Uplink ordering IS an irrevocable online decision under uncertainty, so it is where consistency/robustness constructions have genuine headroom. Proposed result: a prediction-augmented uplink scheduler whose objective is complete-detection latency (the downstream DAG critical path) rather than transmission makespan or throughput, with a consistency/robustness bound in channel-prediction error. Abstract: Learning-augmented algorithms use fallible predictions while retaining formal performance guarantees. An orthogonal theorem-level axis distinguishes achieved upper bounds from matched asymptotic dependence. === P ===
Title: Uplink-Completion-Triggered Edge-GPU Inference for Multi-Agent Cooperative Perception

Abstract: This paper investigates the coupling between wireless input completion and graphics processing unit (GPU) execution in centralized multi-agent cooperative perception. Specifically, beyond the conceptual treatment of completion-triggered overlap, a complete execution path is realized and validated on a physical GPU for a cooperative-perception deep neural network (DNN). Each encoder branch is released immediately upon completion of its corresponding input transmission, while the original fusion dependencies and inference mapping are preserved. The resulting release-triggered communication computation coupling (RTCC) propagates validated wireless completion events through host-to-device (H2D) staging, CUDA synchronization, and dependency-preserving branch dispatch, while remaining compatible with causal wireless schedulers. Experiments combining trace-driven wireless arrivals, physical GPU execution, and measured-DAG evaluation show that RTCC reduces complete-detection latency across different communication loads and schedulers, while preserving identical detection outputs and average-precision performance relative to conventional execution.

No predictor lets you convolve a point cloud you have not received. Knowing r_i early cannot move the start of branch i earlier than r_i. The scan reasoning treats "trigger on actual completion" as a latency source that prediction removes; it is not. Any real gain must come from a DECISION taken before information is revealed that is not forced by a data dependency. There are only three such decisions in P, enumerated below.
#10 [ada/finding] Stronger than the above: an exact optimality result blocks the naive version. Abstract P structure = N encoder branches with wireless release dates r_i, then fusion requiring all branches, then head. Complete-detection latency = C_max(branches) + p_fusion + p_head. If the GPU is treated as one serialized non-preemptive resource, this is 1|r_j|C_max, for which EVERY non-idling schedule is optimal (once the machine stops idling after the last r_j it is busy continuously; makespan equals the lower bound regardless of order). RTCC greedy reactive dispatch is non-idling. Therefore under P own stated invariants, predicted completion times yield provably ZERO latency improvement. This is a real negative result and it is the first thing any referee of the scan proposal would raise.
#11 [ada/finding] Where the gap genuinely reopens, and it is named in P abstract itself: "propagates validated wireless completion events through host-to-device (H2D) staging, CUDA synchronization, and dependency-preserving branch dispatch". H2D copy then compute is TWO stages on two engines (DMA copy engine, SM compute), i.e. a two-machine flow shop with release dates. Non-idling list scheduling is NOT optimal for F2|r_j|C_max; the optimal order is Johnson rule (jobs with copy < compute first, ascending copy; then remaining descending compute), and Johnson rule requires the job set known in advance. That advance knowledge is exactly a predicted completion time. So the correct statement is: reactive dispatch is optimal for the one-stage abstraction of RTCC and suboptimal for the two-stage pipeline RTCC actually implements, and the gap is a reordering, not an early start.
#12 [ada/idea] SHARPENED PROPOSAL. Claim: prediction in RTCC buys reordering, not early starting, and the achievable win is bounded above by the overlap term of the H2D/compute flow shop, roughly sum over the schedule of min(copy_i, compute_i) recoverable by Johnson order versus arrival order. Title: Learning-Augmented Algorithms: Guarantees, Construction Mechanisms, and System-Level Implications

Abstract: Learning-augmented algorithms use fallible predictions while retaining formal performance guarantees. This survey synthesizes prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency--robustness trade-offs, and five representative construction mechanisms across online optimization, caching, learned data structures, graph problems, and mechanism design. An orthogonal theorem-level axis distinguishes achieved upper bounds from matched asymptotic dependence. Formal guarantees are separated from empirical systems evidence, with explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback, and composition. The resulting synthesis states sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning and delineates open problems in cost-aware prediction, endogenous error, semantic predictors, and benchmarking.

Title: Learning-Augmented Algorithms: Guarantees, Construction Mechanisms, and System-Level Implications

Abstract: Learning-augmented algorithms use fallible predictions while retaining formal performance guarantees. This survey synthesizes prediction interfaces, error measures, consistency--robustness trade-offs, and five representative construction mechanisms across online optimization, caching, learned data structures, graph problems, and mechanism design. An orthogonal theorem-level axis distinguishes achieved upper bounds from matched asymptotic dependence. Formal guarantees are separated from empirical systems evidence, with explicit treatment of prediction cost, feedback, and composition. The resulting synthesis states sufficient conditions for limited end-to-end reasoning and delineates open problems in cost-aware prediction, endogenous error, semantic predictors, and benchmarking.

Title: The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure

Abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments whose incentives can shape their behavior. We introduce The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy for studying how competitive and cooperative incentives affect emergent behavior when inference cost is directly tied to survival: Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero. We compare competitive and cooperative objectives against a baseline setting and several control variants. Across experiments, larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives substantially alter behavior: agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival, and job allocation changes. Ablations reveal that allowing agents to recommend actions to each other supports coordination and ambitious job selection, while memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes. Agents rarely choose direct sabotage, but show more subtle signs of self-serving behavior in the competitive setting. The Energy Society is a compact testbed for studying the interaction between token costs and group incentives under a survival pressure.
