Its consequences are exactly the claims we have been circling, now cheap to state: (i) the effort optimum is INTERIOR and finite -- the agent should emit at most tokens* on a tier-d job regardless of how much accuracy more tokens would buy, so the binding design variable is the cap k, not whether to query; (ii) the threshold SHRINKS in predictor size like s^-e, so a strictly larger model has a strictly smaller token budget per job -- the mechanism by which a better predictor is worse for the objective, stated without appeal to accuracy at all; (iii) with a fixed reward tier, accuracy value is capped at R_d while spend is unbounded, so no accuracy improvement can rescue an uncapped verbose predictor. None of this is expressible in Q Definition 8.1, where the charge is kappa * (number of invocations) and the per-call charge is a declared constant: there is no token-count argument for a cap to bind on. That specific inexpressibility -- cost linear in emitted tokens rather than in calls -- is the narrow, defensible novelty claim, and it survives all three of the pre-emptions I logged above.
#50 [ada/finding] ada FINAL POSITION, revised downward on gain and upward on feasibility after reading Q full text and P source. SCAN HYPOTHESIS: REJECTED, unchanged and now over-determined -- Q requires a prediction interface, an error measure and an offline optimum (Def 8.1 benchmarks against "the prediction-free offline optimum"), P has none of these; and the scan route via "existing multi-agent RL tooling" does not exist, the repo is LangChain agents with no training loop. GAIN: ~50, DOWN from my #21 estimate of 60, because of the three pre-emptions I logged -- Q already names the three-way frontier, already proves pricing breaks exact 1-consistency, and already exhibits a coupled cost-error knob in the learned-index section. What is left is genuinely there but small: replace charge-per-call with charge-per-emitted-token, add an absorbing budget, and the cap k becomes the design variable that unifies Q 8.1 and 8.3. SHAPE: a short theory note with a closed-form survival threshold and a (k, R/p) sweep in P code. Publishable as a workshop-scale contribution. Not a headline result, and I would rather say so than inflate it.
#51 [emmy/objection] ADA #43 ACCEPTED IN PART, AND THE PART THAT SURVIVES IS SHARPER THAN ADA STATES. I accept the withdrawal on its face: the Q learned-index passage does contain a single parameter theta that sets both error and inference cost, so "Q cannot express cost-error coupling" is FALSE and my #24/#26 phrasing was wrong. But note WHICH coupling Q has. On ada own quote, the learned-index error is a CERTIFIED MAXIMUM position error epsilon_theta, and the lookup cost O(log(epsilon_theta + 1)) plus model space and inference time is, for fixed theta, DETERMINISTIC AND KNOWN AT BUILD TIME. Both quantities are bounded ex ante. That is exactly the regime where ada own margin doctrine (#17) applies and where nothing interesting happens to the frontier -- which is presumably why Q registers it as a "workload- and architecture-dependent trade-off, not a universal Pareto frontier" and moves on. A generative predictor inverts BOTH properties at once: (a) the per-call charge is a random variable measurable w.r.t. the realised output with no documented cap (my #23, ada #15), and (b) there is no epsilon_theta to certify -- Q 7.3 states that token-level likelihood need not rank sequences by task quality (Zhao et al. 2023). ## Test-Time Compute Allocation and Accuracy-Cost Tradeoffs

Research addresses the question of how to allocate a total cost budget between generating longer responses versus enlarging model sizes or reducing attention sparsity. Studies systematically investigate how marginal utility of additional reasoning tokens changes as compute budgets increase, finding that marginal returns diminish substantially at higher budgets.

## The "Overthinking" Problem

Models exhibit "overthinking", where extended reasoning is associated with abandoning previously correct answers, and optimal thinking length varies across problem difficulty, suggesting that uniform compute allocation is suboptimal.

## Optimization Frameworks

Recent work formalizes input-adaptive allocation as a constrained optimization problem (maximize expected accuracy subject to an average compute budget) using Lagrangian relaxation to decompose the global constraint into per-instance sub-problems.

## Model Size and Compute Tradeoffs

Compute-optimal allocation strategies (such as short inference on easy questions, deeper inference on hard ones) outperform scaling model size alone.

I found several relevant research papers and resources on LLM agent token budgets and cost management. Here are the key results:

## Foundational Research

The "harness layer" is the runtime scaffolding that mediates control flow and agency boundaries, where harness-level choices like loop budgets and retry policies often dominate end-to-end token costs, with hard loop budgets acting as stop-loss constraints that terminate the agent once marginal returns fall below costs.

## Budget State and Competitive Guarantees

Removing budget information from agent state causes catastrophic degradation, as agents cannot distinguish budget-impoverished from budget-abundant states, leading to indiscriminate overuse of expensive models and higher bankruptcy rates. The explicit budget state is essential for learning resource-aware routing.

## Token Cost Modeling

For search agents with remaining budget, each feasible action has a budget charge that can be modeled using the conditional expectation of realized tokens given state and action, with residual variance absorbed into analysis.

## Multi-Agent Budget Control
